item.title: Quadlets: A Developer's Perspective
item.description: A Quick Overview of Using Podman Quadlets For Web Development
item.content:encoded:
Introduction 🔗

Podman's Quadlet feature allows podman containers to be integrated into systemd services.

Why manage containers with systemd? You might argue that containers are better orchestrated with Docker Swarm, Kubernetes, or even Ansible. That is true for larger installations. For a single Linux box or VPS, systemd is probably running on it already. I couldn't summarize it better than Elias Bourgess: it's the control pane you already run.

There are two ways to write Quadlets:

  • INI-style quadlet definitions. An extension of systemd's INI-style config language. This adds sections for things like containers and volumes. This approach is for Linux system administrators who are already familiar with systemd.
  • K8s-style quadlet definitions. These are Kubernetes-style yaml files that define your containers. This approach is clearly aimed at developers and devops folks already familiar with Kubernetes or docker-compose.
Caveats

  • You may be wondering why podman-compose isn't mentioned as an option. While podman-compose is obviously a docker-compose replacement, industry leaders are shying away from supporting it, in favor of podman kube play. More on that here.

  • In order to get k8-style Kubernetes yaml, you need a kube file, which is technically an INI-style file. I'm glossing over that for now, as the bulk of the container definitions are still either expressed in Kubernetes-style YAML or INI.

I'm a developer who's used to docker-compose, so I tried out the k8-style first. That said, curiosity got the better of me, and I wondered what INI-style Quadlet definitions would look like.

Setup 🔗

Here's a minimal setup for a Node.js application (full source code can be found here):

├── app
│   ├── index.js
│   ├── node_modules
│   ├── package.json
│   └── package-lock.json
├── dev
│   ├── example-app-dev.container
│   └── example-app-dev.pod
├── prod
│   ├── Containerfile
│   ├── example-app.build
│   ├── example-app.container
│   └── example-app.pod
└── README.md

The quadlet-specific files here are under the dev and prod subdirectories for development and production, respectively. Here's a look at the ones in dev:

dev/example-app-dev.container:

[Unit]
Description=Example Node.js app

[Container]
Pod=example-app-dev.pod
Image=docker.io/node:24
WorkingDir=/app
Exec=/bin/sh -c "npm i && node --watch index.js"
Volume=../app:/app:Z
Environment=PORT=3001

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

dev/example-app-dev.pod:

[Unit]
Description=Development version of example app

[Pod]
PodName=example-app-dev
ExitPolicy=stop
PublishPort=3001:3001

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
Why wrap one container in a Pod?

You may be wondering why it's wrapped in a Pod. For this example, the Pod is indeed overkill. Once other containers get added to your app (a Postgres db container, a Redis cache layer, reverse-proxy, etc) pods do make it easier to manage containers, and keep them all talking to each other with relative ease. This is because containers on the same pod can all access each other via localhost:PORT, and not worry about whatever host addresses are already in use. Furthermore, at the pod level, only the port that needs access from the outside world (say, a reverse proxy's container port) is published, while the other containers' ports are effectively closed off.

Notes
  1. These aren't the actual files systemd runs

These files get translated (the technical term is "lowered") into other, actual systemd files for systemd to bootstrap. I like to think of the relationship quadlet files to systemd files like the relationship of SASS files to CSS, or React's JSX files to JS. While the syntax of quadlets is similar to what it gets compiled into, it isn't identical. To anyone less familiar with "pure" systemd, it's difficult to distinguish between quadlet and systemd-specific declarations.

  1. Systemd needs application code in certain subdirectories in order to run it

I'm used to cloning repos onto any path on my disk, doing docker-compose up in that repo, and I'm up and running. Unfortunately, the Quadlet workflow isn't quite as straightforward. Systemd ships with most OSs with a predefined set of paths that it looks to discover new services. Quadlets continue that trend.

Fortunately, your application code can live in any directory you'd like, provided that directory gets copied/symlinked over into one of the quadlet discovery paths. A quick ln -sfn "$PWD" ~/.config/containers/systemd/example-app (super intuitive, I know) should do the trick.

  1. Mind the volume mount

Volume=../app:/app:Z mounts your source directory read/write, and the :Z suffix relabels that directory for this one container's private use. That's the right choice for a single container. But if a second container in a different pod ever mounts the same directory, it gets its own SELinux label and one of the two will fail with a "permission denied". If you genuinely intend to share a directory, use :z (shared) instead.

One more thing worth knowing: the above assumes rootless podman (systemctl --user), where the container's root maps to your own user, so anything it writes to ../app stays yours to edit and delete. Run the same directory through sudo podman even once, though, and the files it creates become owned by real root, leaving you reaching for sudo to clean them up.

Dev Workflow: 🔗

  1. Clone the repo.
  2. Find your systemd discovery path. On most systems, that resolves to ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/containers/systemd. So something like ~/.config/containers/systemd. (If you're doing rootless, which I am)
  3. cd into your repo, and link up the repo's subdirs into your quadlet discovery path:
cd project-dir

# symlink the entire project directory over. Note that "example-app" can be anything, and should be uniquely named
# to prevent clashes with other systemd services
ln -sfn "$PWD" ~/.config/containers/systemd/example-app

Now reload systemd with this new application, and confirm all is well

# This rebuilds the quadlets -> actual systemd runtime files
systemctl --user daemon-reload

# Confirm that quadlet picked it up with `podman quadlet list`. If all went well, you'll see your pod listed.
podman quadlet list

# Will probably give you something like
# NAME                       UNIT NAME                    PATH ON DISK                                       STATUS          APPLICATION
# example-app-dev.container  example-app-dev.service      /your/dev-dir/dev/example-app-dev.container        active/running  .dev.app
# example-app-dev.pod        example-app-dev-pod.service  /your/dev-dir/dev/example-app-dev.pod              active/running  .dev.app

# Check the status of the service
systemctl --user status example-app-dev.service

# BONUS: If you'd prefer your services to keep running after you log out (and start at boot), enable lingering for your user
sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER

Now to the actual developing! 🔗

The main source files under app are volume-mounted, so go ahead, start changing index.js, for example. Reload the browser to see your changes.

Deployment Workflow 🔗

If you're deploying to the same system you develop on, then all you're really doing is COPYing the node source files instead of volume-mounting. If you're using Typescript or anything else requiring compilation, you'll have to add that to your Containerfile too.

prod/example-app.container:

[Unit]
Description=Example Node.js app

[Container]
Pod=example-app.pod
Image=example-app.build
Exec=/bin/sh -c "node index.js"
Environment=PORT=3005

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

prod/example-app.pod:

[Unit]
Description=Production version of example app

[Pod]
PodName=example-app-pod
ExitPolicy=stop
PublishPort=3005:3005

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

prod/Containerfile:

FROM docker.io/library/node:24-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY app/ /app/

RUN npm ci

prod/example-app.build:

[Build]
ImageTag=localhost/example-app
File=Containerfile
SetWorkingDirectory=..

You've already linked the production files over, its just a matter of rebuilding.

# Rebuilds any necessary files
systemctl --user daemon-reload

# Start the production service
systemctl --user restart example-app.service

Point a browser at localhost:3005 and you should see your production app!

What about Quadlet Install?

The short answer is, eventually I think we should. I'm only on Podman 5.8.7 (for the latest stable Fedora, as of this writing). On this version, podman quadlet install effectively copies over all your source code files into the base quadlet discovery directory. If you're managing multiple services/quadlets, this would fill up full of .container's and .pods pretty fast! To solve this, they add an .app file to denote which .container files belong to which, but this seems incredibly messy to me. Fortunately, they've changed this in Podman 6, and allow services to be grouped under different directory names (via the --application flag).

In other words, once Fedora upgrades, I'd go with something like podman quadlet install --application="example-app-dev" .. instead.

Final Thoughts 🔗

Honestly, I prefer the k8-style workflow over this. The idea of linking my project subdirectory into an arbitrary system path to start my service just feels so, alien. Even with the changes to Podman 6 and the --application flag, it feels like an odd workflow.

On the flipside, INI-style quadlets feel "closer to the metal". Having everything already written in systemd INI files is a pretty close representation of what actually gets loaded by systemd. There's a movement in the frontend ecosystem which eschews elaborate frameworks for plain "vanilla" javascript, and to just use the platform. I felt like there was a parallel to be found with Quadlets, and that was worth exploring.

item.title: Why Podman?
item.content:encoded:
Podman and its affiliated projects can help manage OCI-compatible containers in several different ways, making it more than a Docker substitute:

  1. Licensing

Podman is Apache-2.0 licensed. Basically, it's open source and can be used by an unlimited number of users for free. If you like using Docker Desktop, its Podman equivalent is free and open source as well, and won't ask you to pay if your company gets past a certain size.

  1. Security

Podman allows its containers to be rootless. What is rootless? It means there isn't one central process (daemon) that's in charge of all your containers. Not one central process that could crash and bring down all your containers, not one central process that could get compromised, and start acting maliciously. To be fair, Docker has rootless mode now too, so if rootless is your only attraction, just switch to that.

  1. Integration with SystemD

Podman's Quadlets facilitate integrating with systemd as well. Why bother integrating with systemd? Your web app is probably running on a server with Linux, and that version of Linux is probably using systemd. systemd isn't technically part of Linux itself, but it's the unofficial standard init system for most Linux distros, including Fedora, Ubuntu, and many others. Unless your server is running Slackware, integrating with systemd is a no-brainer.

  1. Pods

As the name suggests, Podman works with sets of pods. Although Docker has no equivalent feature, pods aren't specific to Podman either, as the concept was inspired from Kubernetes. Pods allow containers to be grouped together and given their own network namespace. Once containers are grouped into “pods”, those pods can be started/restarted together, like podman pod start my-app.

This feature is less geared towards developers, more so system admins/devops who manage lots of containers. That said, they're easy to set up, and alleviate some of the tedium associated with spinning up/down large numbers of containers.

I've been using Podman for a few years now, and overall I've found it a completely acceptable replacement for Docker. That said, I've found most of the tutorials/resources (and subsequently, AI) have described Podman from a more system-admin/devops workflow, not a web developer workflow. So in the next few posts, I'm going to outline some ways I've found to work with Podman containers. Some of them will be fairly familiar (like podman-compose), while others are much newer (like a Kubernetes-style “kube” file).
